items.text:
We are working on the FG (Finished Goods) screen in SAP Public Cloud, where we need to control authorization based on different fields and operations. 
 One of the fields in the FG screen is a Shift dropdown. This dropdown has 3 possible values: 
 DAY – Day Shift 
 NGT – Night Shift 
 GEN – General Shift 
 The requirement is that the user should only be authorized for the Shift values that are maintained in their Business Role. 
 For example, suppose a Business Role has the following authorization: 
 Application: FG 
 Operation: 0010 
 Shift: GEN 
 In this case, when the user accesses the FG screen, the expected authorization should be: 
 GEN → Authorized 
 DAY → Not Authorized 
 NGT → Not Authorized 
 Technically, we have created a Global Authorization Class for performing the authorization checks, a Field-Level Authorization Class for checking authorization for individual fields, and a Behavior Implementation Class that calls these authorization methods and returns the result to the FG screen. 
 The issue we are facing is with the actual authorization check. 
 During debugging, we are checking each Shift value separately. For example: 
 GEN → AUTHORITY-CHECK → sy-subrc = 0 → Authorized 
 This is correct because GEN is assigned in the Business Role. 
 But when we check: 
 DAY → AUTHORITY-CHECK → sy-subrc = 0 → Authorized 
 and 
 NGT → AUTHORITY-CHECK → sy-subrc = 0 → Authorized 
 These are also returning authorized, even though DAY and NGT were not assigned in the Business Role. 
 We also tested the standard AUTHORITY-CHECK directly during debugging, without using our authorization wrapper method. Even there, DAY and NGT are returning: 
 sy-subrc = 0 
 So it does not appear to be an issue with our wrapper logic or with assigning rv_ok = X. 
 We are seeing the same type of behavior with some of the other authorization fields as well: values that are not explicitly maintained in the Business Role are still passing the authorization check.

 IF iv_inchg IS NOT INITIAL

 rv_ok = xsdbool( sy-subrc = 0 ).

items.title: SAP Named a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape for AI-Enabled Direct Spend
items.author: Fang Chang
items.text:
SAP has been positioned in the Leader Category of the 2026 IDC MarketScape for AI-Enabled Direct Spend Vendor Assessment .* 
 Optimize procurement and invoicing processes through supplier collaboration 

 Learn how 

 We believe this recognition reflects SAP’s long-term investment in helping manufacturers connect sourcing, engineering, planning, and supplier collaboration on a single foundation. 

 Direct materials procurement doesn’t get enough credit for how hard it actually is. Unlike indirect spend, direct materials sit at the intersection of engineering, planning, finance, and supplier relationships—often all at once. A design change triggers a sourcing event. A commodity price spike ripples into contract terms. A supplier quality issue lands on the production floor before procurement even knows it happened. 

 The organizations that manage this well don’t just have good sourcing tools. They have connected systems, trusted data, and the ability to act quickly when conditions change. Solving for that complexity is what SAP’s direct spend portfolio is built to do. 

 Connecting design, sourcing, and execution 

 SAP’s direct spend offering is built with an industry-specific lens. A cookie-cutter approach to procurement business processes does not work for direct materials. 

 An engineering-oriented industry like automotive or aerospace, where a design change can trigger a sourcing event, has fundamentally different needs than a brand- or asset-oriented industry such as consumer goods or chemicals, where commodity exposure and supplier scale dominate. SAP builds for both, with purpose-built offerings tuned to how each actually works. 

 What our offerings share is a single, unbroken data model running from new product introduction through sourcing, contract award, and purchase order execution, all within SAP Business Suite: no bolt-on connectors, no manual handoffs between systems. 

 This matters more than it might seem. Data fragmentation across the design-to-source-to-settle workflow remains one of the biggest barriers to AI delivering real value in direct spend. When procurement decisions are connected to engineering, planning, supplier, and financial data on a shared foundation, AI has meaningful context to work with. 

 A network and ecosystem that extends the core 

 The sourcing suites are the center of gravity, but what surrounds them is equally important for manufacturers managing complex, multi-tier supply chains. 

 SAP Business Network connects millions of trading partners across roughly 190 countries, with more than US$7.7 trillion in annual commerce flowing through it. The network supports forecast collaboration, purchase order execution, inventory management, logistics visibility, quality processes, and supplier communication. For global manufacturers managing complex supply chains, that scale can be operationally significant. 

 Customers are already seeing the benefits of a more integrated approach to direct spend. For example, global a u tomotive supplier Multimatic selected SAP’s direct materials sourcing solution because of its close integration with core ERP processes, including bill of materials management, production planning, and cost calculation. By connecting sourcing more closely to product development and manufacturing workflows, the company is helping procurement, engineering, and suppliers work from the same foundation throughout the product life cycle. 

 Additional SAP capabilities extend the process further across product development, commodity management, supply planning, supplier collaboration, financing, and analytics. Together, these capabilities help organizations manage direct spend as part of an integrated process that spans from early design collaboration through supplier payment, supported by a unified data foundation. 

 Taken together, these capabilities span a much broader scope than traditional sourcing software, from early design collaboration through supplier payment, all governed on SAP Business Data Cloud as a unified analytics foundation. 

 Where AI stands today, and where it’s going 

 Today, SAP delivers AI-powered supplier and item recommendations, invoice data extraction, category strategy insights, supplier risk scoring, and Joule capabilities embedded throughout the suite. These are production capabilities already helping customers streamline procurement processes. 

 Looking ahead, SAP plans to expand its AI capabilities across the direct spend life cycle, with new agentic experiences focused on areas such as market intelligence, supplier discovery, RFx orchestration, negotiation support, contract authoring, and supply chain impact analysis. These innovations will be delivered through Joule Work and Joule Studio 2.0, a no-code/low-code environment built on SAP Business AI that enables organizations to create and manage agents grounded in live business data and end-to-end process context. 

 The foundation underneath this road map is what makes it credible. Agents are only as good as the data and process context they can access. When that foundation is fragmented across disconnected systems, AI adds noise as often as it adds value. When it’s unified, agents can execute with greater relevance and accuracy. 

 Who this is built for 

 The SAP Ariba offering foo direct spend works with any ERP backend, with the added benefit of integrating out of the box with SAP Cloud ERP. For aerospace and defense customers with data sovereignty requirements, SAP offers deployment options for sovereign cloud that few vendors in this space support. For brand- and asset-oriented enterprises, a consolidated source-to-pay platform spanning both direct and indirect spend can simplify governance while reducing complexity. 

 For manufacturers operating complex global supply chains, the value of a natively integrated approach is straightforward: fewer manual handoffs, better visibility across functions, faster response to disruptions, and AI that can draw on connected business data rather than isolated point solutions. 

 What this recognition means to us 

 We’re grateful to the customers and partners whose real-world feedback shapes how we build these products. We believe an IDC MarketScape recognition reflects their experiences as much as it reflects our road map, and we don’t take that lightly. 

 This recognition energizes us. For more than 50 years, SAP has helped organizations run their most critical business processes, and direct spend is one of the areas where that experience comes together most clearly. We’ll continue investing in deeper integration, broader network capabilities, trusted AI, and the industry expertise our customers rely on. We’re grateful to the customers and partners that continue to help shape these solutions and help us deliver meaningful innovation across the direct spend life cycle.

items.title: What Implementation Teams Wish Organizations Knew About Enterprise RFPs
items.author: Drew Messinger-Michaels
items.text:
RFPs are common in the world of enterprise software. Truly successful ones, less so. 

 Well-run RFPs get right to the heart of requirements, match enterprises with the right solutions, and build solid plans to launch those solutions. Disorganized RFPs significantly lengthen the decision-making process without adding the intended value. 

 So what separates an effective RFP from the rest? 

 Let’s delve into a systems integrator’s perspective of what can go right, what can go wrong, and what purposes the whole process can actually serve. 

 Throughout this article, “RFP” means the document a business creates to solicit responses from vendors. “RFP response” means the reply to an RFP from a vendor. 

 Why do organizations still run RFPs? 

 According to Michael Andrion, account executive and partnerships for BASE1, “There are really three different reasons for running an RFP: to select a vendor, to describe the problem that needs to be solved, and to end up with a well-scoped plan for solving it.” 

 Let’s break that down in a bit more detail: 

 Select a vendor: You’d be surprised at how many RFPs end without a vendor decision being made. An RFP may fail to result in a decision for multiple reasons, including an unexpected business acquisition, a change in budget, timeline issues, and more. Thorough preparation and buy-in from stakeholders can help ensure a successful outcome. 

 Describe the problem that needs to be solved: An RFP can be a highly effective tool for internal interrogation, so you can clarify what problems stakeholders truly want to address. 

 Build a well-scoped plan for solving it: When done well, the RFP process will give you answers to questions about timelines, pricing, and staffing. 

 RFPs can be driven by compliance requirements or internal governance, but can also act as useful early discovery activities. Organizations use RFPs as a sort of first gate, or first hurdle, to see which vendors are worth having deeper discussions with. 

 What makes a good RFP, and what makes a bad one? 
 Find the right martech vendor. Get the sample questions. 

 Learn more 

 What often separates a good RFP from a bad one is finding the right level of detail . 

 If the RFP questions are completely generic, the business might not learn what it actually needs to know. Simultaneously, too many questions can easily result in counter-productive situations where RFPs written by AI receive responses written by AI, which are then summarized by AI. 

 You need well-crafted questions that are unique to your business. That way vendors can supply responses that your experts will actually read, helping them reach the right decision for your business. 

 How can an RFP achieve a level of open communication? 

 Open communication between a business and prospective vendors creates better outcomes. 

 However, there’s a challenge that comes with finding the right level of detail: highly detailed, nuanced questions often invite exactly the kind of deeper, looser discussion that a formalized RFP process precludes. To whatever degree possible (and that degree varies for good reasons, especially for regulated industries), think about whether the formality of the process is preventing the kind of honest dialogue that ultimately leads to better decisions. 

 Two tips when it comes to RFPs: 

 Ask yourself and your stakeholders whether you really need to go through the complete RFP process or whether 1:1 meetings and demos may be the right route. 

 If you do go through the RFP process , plan on doing a follow-up question and answer session afterward, and/or down-select to vendors from which you’d like a more personalized demonstration. 

 What does a business need to know before starting an RFP process? 

 RFPs run more smoothly when the issuing company has already done some data gathering. 

 Come to the table with: 

 Key metrics 

 Expectations around SLAs 

 A ballpark sense of budget 

 With this information, you’ll be able to qualify (and disqualify) the right candidates more efficiently and effectively. 

 Before starting an RFP, be sure you have time to run one. It’s a time-consuming process, so start with your preferred go-live date and work backwards from there. Here’s a general timeline from the Martech RFP Guide : 

 Do all RFPs have to follow the traditional format? 

 In the past couple of years, there’s been an interesting trend in the field: namely reversing or inverting the traditional RFP process. Rather than beginning with a detailed spreadsheet of requirements before moving to a demo phase, organizations first hold short demonstrations, introductory meetings, and high-level pricing discussions. 

 This demo-first approach allows both sides to evaluate cultural fit, communication style, technical dealbreakers, and business understanding before investing significant time in detailed documentation. 

 What distinguishes a strong vendor? 

 After the RFP response comes the evaluation. The right vendor isn’t just the one who ticks all the functional and technical boxes and the lowest price tag, important as those factors are. 

 The right vendor is willing to become a student of your business and dig into a day in the life of your stakeholders. A well-structured RFP can show you which vendors are willing to do exactly that and to step outside of their comfort zones when and where you’ll need them to. 

 Ask yourself if the vendor just went through the motions, or if they actually understand your unique business needs. 

 What distinguishes a strong implementation partner? 

 The strongest implementation partners demonstrate a clear understanding of the customer’s business before tying those requirements to any specific technology. 

 Here are the green flags to look for in a strong implementation partner. The partner should: 

 Arrive prepared 

 Ask thoughtful questions 

 Share relevant customer stories 

 Focus on being true partners rather than rote order-takers 

 If you’re involving partners in your RFP process, challenge them to do some real analysis. Challenging questions are a good indicator that the business is truly invested in making the implementation a success. 

 Final takeaway: it never hurts to ask a question! 

 At its best, an enterprise CX RFP is an opportunity to improve communication, surface assumptions, encourage honest dialogue, and make better-informed decisions before implementation begins. Enter the process with eyes open and schedule planned, gather your key data and metrics before kicking off, and build a core set of meaningful questions. 

 Have deeper discussions as soon as they’re relevant. Don’t be afraid to ask for numbers. And to whatever degree you’re able, shape the process to your organization’s specific priorities. Asking the right questions goes a long way toward getting the best possible answers. 

 For even more insights, watch this podcast session , and for more RFP process best practices and sample questions, check out the Martech RFP Guide .

items.title: SAP AppHaus Network Partner Bluestonex Builds the Bridge: From Inspiration to Hands-On AI Innovation
items.author: Imke Vierjahn
items.text:
With so many new opportunities brought about by artificial intelligence, companies need to make informed decisions, prioritize, and invest wisely in new AI technology. Not everything that is possible today makes sense in their specific business reality. That is why customer enablement is a crucial part of the global SAP AppHaus Network and its partners. Here’s a recent example of customer enablement provided by SAP AppHaus Network partner Bluestonex . 

 In early July 2026, SAP AppHaus Network partner Bluestonex invited customers to an immersive hands-on workshop day at the Bluestonex AppHaus Oswestry, Shropshire, UK. The focus was placed on two industries: retail and supply chain. During the event, attendees watched inspiring demos of new SAP AI capabilities powered by the SAP Experience Center and took part in interactive sessions to experience industry innovation and learn along the pragmatic, human-centered innovation approach. 
 Experience a new way of working with the Autonomous Enterprise 

 Learn more 

 Different showcases for retail and supply chain 

 Two different showcases shed light on different applications and scenarios from the retail and supply chain industries. 

 The first showed how data can be surfaced and acted on meaningfully via the use of AI and smart application functions including SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) and Bluestonex’s flagship master data management and governance solution, Maextro. The second showed different supply chain and warehouse use cases from the retail and manufacturing industry, where the participants could experience the demo with physical mobile devices and interactive stock movements as if they were in the warehouse setting itself. 

 Two work streams to explore AI-infused innovation 

 After learning about the art of the possible brought about by the latest SAP Business AI solutions of the Autonomous Enterprise, the workshop attendees split into two work streams to explore different aspects of AI-infused innovation: 

 The first group went through a process of rapid ideation and prototype development with a fast-paced innovation approach. Participants got hands-on, creating both low-fidelity and high-fidelity designs. To do so, they were shown how different AI tools, such as Joule Studio , are changing the way applications are built. 

 To explore the skills needed for successful AI adoption and to address the culture shift, the second session used LEGO® Serious Play® and explored the human side of AI transformation. The method is used for skill-building exercises to then tackle a central challenge: building a model that represents how AI could fundamentally change an existing business. The participants learned a set of guiding principles for AI that they can apply in their day-to-day business. 

 SAP AppHaus Network partners acting as front-runners 

 The workshop is a good example of how SAP partners such as Bluestonex act as front-runners when it comes to exploring the Autonomous Enterprise and adopting AI in a meaningful way. During the workshop, experts helped customer teams identify appropriate use cases, design a concept for an AI agent, and create a real business solution that can be built with the latest SAP technology, encouraging and enabling them to conquer this new environment with all its opportunities. The guiding workshop principle was to create value in their respective company context. 

 The feedback given by some of the participants seems to acknowledge that: 

 “Wow. Mind blown! Great team showing the art of the possible. Excellent.” 

 “Really great day overall. I always love the real-world scenarios. The hands-on sessions were a highlight, and it’s a great visual display of what’s possible.” 

 “Great way to generate ideas, meeting other people, engaging format. The real-world scenarios stood out.” 

 “The space itself—the Bluestonex church—was a highlight. Love the SAP Experience Center content on the big, beautiful screen.” 

 Looking back from two perspectives 
 Workshop scene at Bluestonex AppHaus Shropshire, UK, with Dan Barton, Bluestonex co-founder, and Tobias Gollwitzer, SAP AppHaus. 

 Richard Henry, head of Growth, SAP BTP, Data, & Innovation at Bluestonex, looks back: “The addition of the latest demo content powered by the SAP Experience Center to Bluestonex’s industry workshop model marks another step in our mission to help customers realize the Autonomous Enterprise. By combining the latest innovation stories, industry experiences, and SAP Business AI with proven SAP AppHaus methodologies, we move beyond inspiration to action. Through hands-on workshops, design thinking, and immersive experiences, organizations can explore, validate, and prioritize real business opportunities. In the end, our focus remains the same: we want to turn innovation with the latest SAP solutions into practical outcomes and adoption, all for the benefit of our customers.” 

 Tobias Gollwitzer, senior director and regional lead EMEA, SAP AppHaus Walldorf, concludes: “This workshop is just another proof of the exceptional agility, the dynamic approach, and attitude of our SAP AppHaus Network partner in the UK. The team invites and motivates SAP customers to be among the first to conquer new SAP industry-specific technologies, grasp and move towards SAP’s Autonomous Enterprise solutions to their best advantage.”

items.title: The Autonomous Enterprise, Unfiltered: Lessons From 16 Executive Conversations
items.author: Benedikt Gieger
items.text:
Since SAP Sapphire in May , SAP CEO Christian Klein has positioned the Autonomous Enterprise as the operating model for organizations that will lead the decade ahead, a model in which AI agents reason, decide, and execute inside the workflows that run the business. 

 For many enterprise leaders, however, the gap between strategic ambition and operational reality has remained frustratingly wide. That gap is exactly what the Autonomous Enterprise podcast set out to close. 

 Embed from open.spotify.com 

 Click the button below to load the content from open.spotify.com. 

 Load this embed 
 Always allow open.spotify.com 

 Launched on June 1, 2026, the weekly series has now published 16 episodes spanning three format categories: SAP Deep Dives, with executive leaders on strategy and product; Customer Deep Dives, with companies narrating their own transformation journeys; and Industry Deep Dives, with selected external voices shaping entire industries. 

 Available on Spotify, Apple Music, and all major podcast platforms, as well as on SAP channels and LinkedIn, the show has rapidly established itself as a direct and candid voice on enterprise AI adoption. 

 What the first 16 episodes reveal 

 Across more than a dozen conversations—with guests that include SAP executives, global customers, and external thought leaders—four themes emerge with striking consistency. 

 Autonomous enterprise is available today, not tomorrow 

 In episode 13, Uma Rani, president and chief product officer for SAP Cloud ERP Private, plainly stated that the Autonomous Enterprise is not a future road map item; it is available now for customers on the 2025 and 2023 releases. The show’s earliest episodes reinforced this framing: Peter Maier, leading Strategic Customer Engagements in the Office of the CEO, opened episode one by grounding the SAP Sapphire vision in practical execution, while Manoj Swaminathan used episode three to unpack the architecture of SAP Autonomous Suite, the layer where AI assistants and agents begin to execute end-to-end processes. 

 The decisive advantage is business context, not model capability 

 Michael Ameling, formerly president of the SAP Business AI Platform at SAP, explained in episode four how SAP Knowledge Graph and domain models, combined with frontier models including Anthropic’s Claude, give enterprise AI the semantic grounding that generic LLMs lack. The platform brings together 50 years of SAP process knowledge to enable agents that act relevantly, reliably, and responsibly—three conditions every guest returned to when discussing trustworthy AI at scale. 

 Transformation is a people and change management challenge as much as a technology one 

 In episode two, Ferose V R articulated a shift from humans adapting to systems toward systems adapting to humans, through agents that understand context and intent. Sanjay Kulkarni, senior vice president and global head of Global Delivery Hub at SAP, brought a practitioner’s precision to episode 12: his 12,500-strong services organization measures AI value not by deployment volume, but by measurable business outcomes and the readiness of the people responsible for them. The same message came from Geoff Scott, CEO and chief community champion of Americas’ SAP Users’ Group (ASUG), in episode eight: trust, skill development, and genuine human-AI collaboration are the variables that separate transformations that scale from those that stall. 

 Geographic diversity shapes adoption, but the direction is universal 

 In episode nine, SAP Labs India Managing Director Sindhu Gangadharan mapped how Indian enterprises are approaching autonomous capabilities: fast adoption, high ambition, and a particular emphasis on workforce readiness. Manos Raptopoulos, global president of Customer Success, Europe, APAC, Middle East, and Africa, covered in episode 11 what AI ambition looks like from Frankfurt to Fukuoka, illustrating how regional context varies while the structural imperatives remain the same. And SAP EMEA President Augusta Spinelli used episode five to define the two concrete paths to the Autonomous Enterprise—RISE with SAP and SAP GROW—as well as what agent-led transformation looks like from an execution standpoint. 

 In addition, customer episodes add the texture that strategy alone cannot provide. Achim Loebke from Uniper and Daniele Tedesco from Essity both shared in-depth, unfiltered accounts of what AI transformation looks like from the inside, including the organizational friction, the decisions that require human judgment, and the early indicators of measurable impact. These conversations, deliberately not positioned as product showcases, have consistently drawn the highest listener engagement. 

 Why this series matters for the SAP ecosystem 

 The Autonomous Enterprise podcast fills a gap by offering candid, executive-level conversations where the honest complexity of AI adoption is treated as the point, not a problem to be managed. Its target audience—CIOs, CDOs, COOs, CFOs, and senior transformation leads—are precisely the people making the investment and governance decisions that will determine how quickly SAP customers move from AI ambition to AI execution. 

 With more than 40 episodes planned for its first year, the series is building a cumulative body of insight that serves both as a reference for practitioners navigating their own transformation journeys and as evidence of the breadth and depth of SAP’s engagement with its customer community. 

 New episodes drop weekly; listen on Spotify, Apple Music, and all major podcast platforms.

items.title: SAP Recognized as a Leader in the Inaugural Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Workforce Management Technology

items.text:
Organizations today face growing pressure to navigate labor shortages, evolving employee expectations, changing skills requirements, and increasing operational complexity. As these challenges converge—across factory floors, service centers, project teams, and global operations—workforce management is becoming more than an operational necessity. It’s becoming a strategic foundation for workforce transformation. Gartner predicts that by 2030, 70% of organizations will adopt AI-enabled workforce management technology to decrease managers’ administrative workload by an average of four to six hours per week, optimize operations, and enhance employee experience. 

 That’s why we’re proud that SAP has been recognized as a Leader in the inaugural Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Workforce Management Technology . 

 We believe this recognition reflects SAP’s commitment to helping organizations connect workforce operations, workforce intelligence, and business outcomes through a unified human capital management (HCM) platform. 
 This graphic was published by Gartner, Inc. as part of a larger research document and should be evaluated in the context of the entire document. The Gartner document is available upon request from www.sap.com/products/hcm/workforce-management.html . 

 Workforce management in the era of Autonomous HCM 

 As organizations prepare for the next era of work, leaders need more than scheduling tools and time systems. They need a connected understanding of their workforce. 

 Who is available? What skills are needed? Where are emerging labor gaps? How can workforce decisions better support business priorities? 

 These questions sit at the intersection of workforce management and workforce strategy. 

 That’s why workforce management plays an important role in SAP’s vision for Autonomous HCM . At its core, Autonomous HCM is about helping organizations move more quickly from workforce insight to action. 

 Workforce management plays a critical role in that vision by providing the operational data and workforce visibility needed to make more informed decisions. 

 By bringing workforce management together with core HR, payroll, talent management, and workforce planning, SAP SuccessFactors solutions help organizations gain a more connected view of their workforce, streamline operations, and make more informed workforce decisions. 
 Simplify and enhance your everyday workforce operations with SAP SuccessFactors solutions 

 Learn more 

 Advancing workforce management 

 SAP continues to invest in capabilities that help organizations connect scheduling, absence management, time and attendance, workforce planning, and workforce decision-making. Recent innovations include the general availability of SAP SuccessFactors Workforce Scheduling , helping manufacturing and production organizations align labor demand, workforce availability, employee skills, and compliance requirements within a more connected scheduling experience. 

 We also recently introduced a new Workforce Management Assistant , which helps employees and managers complete common workforce management tasks—like automatically pre-filling time sheets, validating entries against compliance requirements in real time, and answering policy questions—cutting employee time sheet completion effort by up to 40% and HR service tickets by up to 20%. 

 For professional services organizations, this focus on streamlining time extends further. The new consolidated timesheet experience across SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP SuccessFactors Time Tracking helps unify project time and HR attendance in a single flow from resource planning to revenue recognition. 

 From frontline workers on the production floor to project professionals, these capabilities reflect SAP’s commitment to industry-specific depth in workforce management. 

 Beyond workforce operations, SAP recently introduced new workforce planning capabilities within SAP Enterprise Planning , helping leaders connect workforce decisions directly to HR, business, and financial priorities through a unified planning foundation. 

 In addition, AI-enabled organizational modeling capabilities can support scenario planning and impact analysis, enabling business and HR leaders to evaluate organizational changes and workforce decisions before they are implemented. 

 Together, these innovations help organizations connect workforce operations, workforce planning, and workforce decisions in new ways, supporting SAP’s broader vision for Autonomous HCM. 

 Delivering meaningful outcomes 

 Organizations across more than 126 countries and 29 industries are using SAP SuccessFactors workforce management solutions to help improve workforce visibility, streamline time and scheduling processes, strengthen compliance, and create better experiences for employees and managers.

items.title: The AI Governance Gap: Why Responsible AI Drives Adoption
items.author: Matthias Medert
items.text:
In conversations with customers across industries, trust is the barrier to AI adoption that comes up more often. Leaders and organizations need confidence that AI systems will perform reliably and remain accountable for suggested business actions, protecting sensitive data and treating people fairly. Ethical AI deployment closes that gap. When a system is technically robust, legally aligned, and ethically governed, customers, partners, and employees can scale it with confidence rather than caution. 
 SAP is dedicated to delivering relevant, reliable, and responsible AI solutions 

 Read the SAP Global AI Ethics policy 

 SAP has updated the SAP Global AI Ethics policy to version 3.0 , reflecting the fast-changing AI landscape and lessons drawn from deep-dive interviews with more than 50 international experts. The revision reflects concrete changes made to strengthen the ethical safeguards, accountability, and safety measures within enterprise AI adoption, addressing the substance of business leaders’ concerns, not just the perception of them. 

 Our approach to AI rests on three words: relevant, reliable, and responsible. For SAP, ethical deployment isn’t a regulatory checkbox or a marketing layer; it’s the foundation that makes the Autonomous Enterprise possible, where intelligent agents coordinate and execute complex workflows while humans remain firmly in control. 

 Three disciplines for responsible AI 

 Ethics sit at the very center of SAP’s broader social sustainability agenda, where responsible AI depends on three disciplines working together, not in isolation: 

 Ethics define our values . We set clear moral boundaries for how technology should serve humanity. 

 Security protects our systems and data . We safeguard core enterprise assets against emerging cyber threats and vulnerabilities. 

 Compliance ensures legal alignment . We are proactively preparing for global regulatory standards like the EU AI Act. 

 Together, they help teams assess whether an AI use case should proceed, what safeguards it requires, and who is accountable for its performance after deployment, ensuring that as business processes become automated, human dignity, fairness, and agency remain intact. 

 Ethics underpin the Autonomous Enterprise 

 As AI shifts from assisting people to acting on their behalf, the governance question becomes more urgent. The Autonomous Enterprise represents a repositioning where AI agents no longer just make recommendations, but execute business processes end-to-end, across finance, supply chain, procurement, HR, and customer experience. As CEO Christian Klein put it, “For the mission-critical processes of our customers, ‘almost right’ just isn’t good enough.” 

 That’s precisely why ethics and governance can’t be an afterthought bolted onto agentic AI. They have to be the foundation it runs on. Every action an SAP agent takes is logged and traceable, so organizations can always know what an agent did, why it did it, and what data it used. Autonomy without that foundation is just an experiment; autonomy built on it is an operating model organizations can trust at scale. 

 Translating principles into practice 

 The SAP Global AI Ethics policy, grounded in UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, governs the development, deployment, use, and sale of every AI system across the company. SAP’s updated AI Ethics Handbook translates these principles into day-to-day practice. It helps give engineering and product teams a one-stop reference for applying the policy’s guiding principles, from fairness and non-discrimination to human oversight and sustainability. 

 To bridge the gap between high-level principles and day-to-day engineering, we embed strict operational checkpoints into our product life cycle: 

 Mandatory AI ethics impact assessments : Every SAP AI use case must undergo a rigorous evaluation before reaching deployment, based on 10 AI ethics principles. Use cases receive a risk score and the SAP’s AI Ethics Office helps product teams enforce mitigation measures and safeguards in place. Depending on the risks involved, some use cases go through several review steps and may be escalated to the SAP Global AI Ethics steering committee for a final decision. 

 Human oversight by design : SAP systems are built to ensure humans remain in control of critical decisions . 

 Internal accountability : Compliance is non-negotiable across SAP. All employees acknowledge the policy, and the rules apply universally, including to internal, self-developed AI applications built using tools like Hyperspace AI or Claude Code. 

 The process provides clear guardrails that are visible to SAP’s stakeholders, including customers and employees. 

 Leading the industry in AI governance 

 The demand for transparent governance is urgent, and independent evaluations highlight significant gaps in corporate readiness worldwide. In benchmark research by the Thomson Reuters Foundation and UNESCO assessing 2,972 companies, SAP was among the only 12.4% found to maintain an explicit policy ensuring human oversight in AI systems. 

 SAP’s leadership in ethical AI has earned external recognition: the company was named a leading positive example in the Collective Impact Coalition for Ethical AI Progress Report . SAP is also an active participant in the World Economic Forum’s Global Coalition for AI and Social Innovation , convened by the Global Alliance for Social Entrepreneurship in partnership with the Schwab Foundation. Working alongside leading technology companies and social innovators, SAP is helping shape responsible AI deployment to accelerate social impact and extend the benefits of enterprise AI to organizations tackling the world’s most complex challenges. 

 The broader landscape shows how much ground the industry still has to cover. Data from the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment (CSA) shows that only 36% of responding companies have a dedicated or integrated AI policy. Research from BSI paints a similar picture: just 27% of global businesses currently factor their AI footprint into their broader sustainability strategies, a notable gap given the surging energy demands of AI data centers. 

 Unlocking sustainable growth 

 Ethical AI goes beyond risk mitigation and regulatory readiness—it drives tangible economic value. By ensuring fairness, transparency, and robust data privacy, organizations protect their brand reputation while empowering their workforce to perform at their highest level. 

 When AI coordinates, executes, and optimizes routine business processes within an ethical context, employees are freed from manual tasks to focus on strategy, creativity, and human connection. This synergy between human potential and artificial intelligence forms the backbone of sustainable enterprise growth. 

 Organizations that understand this will reap the rewards as regulations tighten and societal expectations increase. However, ethical AI only becomes a reality when we work together. We look forward to continuing to work alongside our customers and partners as we embrace one of the most important challenges and competitive advantages in the AI era. 

 Read the SAP Global AI Ethics policy version 3.0 . Find out more about the Autonomous Enterprise . 

 Matthias Medert is head of Sustainability at SAP.

items.title: Can Agentic AI Bridge the Gap with Trusted Enterprise Data?
items.author: Tim Clark
items.text:
As artificial intelligence moves beyond providing information and recommendations, enterprise software is becoming more capable of reasoning, making decisions, and taking action across business processes. 
 SAP Reltio in SAP Business Data Cloud: Build a trusted system of context 

 Learn how 

 It’s a noticeable shift that could fundamentally change how enterprises operate. But according to Manish Sood, CEO of Reltio, an SAP company , and co-author of Agentic Intelligence , it also exposes a challenge companies have wrestled with for decades: fragmented, inconsistent, and poorly connected data. 

 “There is tremendous enthusiasm around agentic AI right now, and for good reason,” said Sood. “Almost every company is experimenting with it in some form or the other. But there is a very significant gap between ambition and underlying readiness.” 

 Research conducted by Harvard Business Review Analytic Services underscores that readiness gap: 94% of organizations surveyed are exploring or implementing agentic AI, while only 15% believe their data foundation is truly ready. 

 “An AI demo can tolerate a lot of imperfections and gaps in the data,” said Sood. “An AI agent operating inside a real business context cannot. The moment we give software the ability to make decisions or to take action, the quality, timeliness, and context of underlying data becomes much more consequential.” 

 AI highlights legacy data challenges 

 Sood believes fragmentation, trust, and governance are three recurring barriers when it comes to AI adoption. Because data remains scattered across hundreds or even thousands of enterprise systems, governance models built for traditional enterprise systems must evolve for an environment in which AI agents can initiate actions. 

 While these are familiar challenges, the speed and autonomy AI introduces is much different. 

 Historically, humans have compensated for fragmented systems via tapping into institutional knowledge. Employees know which spreadsheet to check, which colleague to call, or which exception to make. AI agents do not inherently possess that organizational context. 

 “If a human has incomplete information, we can often recognize it, ask another question, or find someone who knows the history,” said Sood. “In comparison, an autonomous agent may simply act.” 

 The question for enterprises therefore shifts from whether they can build an AI agent to whether they can trust the environment in which that agent operates. 

 From digital filing cabinets to connected intelligence 

 Many organizations still operate around what Sood refers to as the “filing cabinet” model. When businesses digitized, individual functions created their own systems for marketing, finance, sales, supply chain, service, and human resources. Moving those systems to the cloud did not necessarily eliminate the underlying silos. 

 “The intelligence age requires us to move from storing information to connecting that information,” he said. 

 This connected foundation supports what Sood and his co-author describe as “co-agency,” a new relationship between people and intelligent machines. 

 Historically, enterprise technology followed a relatively simple model: humans made decisions and machines executed them. AI changes that equation. Machines can contribute speed, scale, pattern recognition, and continuous operation, while people provide judgment, experience, accountability, and an understanding of nuance. 

 “If the human sees one version of the customer and the agent sees another, you don’t have co-agency; you have conflict,” said Sood. 

 Turning insight into action 

 These implications extend beyond technology architecture as agentic intelligence requires companies to rethink strategy, investment, workflows, governance, and the relationship between people and machines. It’s a notable shift that moves from insight to action. 

 “Insight by itself does not create economic value. Action does,” Sood shared. 

 For example, predicting that a piece of industrial equipment is likely to fail can provide valuable information. But an intelligent system capable of coordinating maintenance, locating the necessary parts, and scheduling service before the failure occurs can potentially transform that insight directly into a business outcome. In order for this to happen, however, trusted information needs to be available when and where decisions happen. 

 According to Sood, four responsibilities are necessary for organizations preparing for this environment: 

 Connect critical enterprise data. 

 Contextualize it with relationships, history, policies, and interactions. 

 Operationalize that trusted context at the point of decision. 

 Govern how AI agents act. 

 “Define where an agent can act, where a human needs to intervene, how decisions are traced, and how systems learn from mistakes,” Sood explained. “The goal isn’t simply to make more data available to AI. The goal is to make the enterprise understandable through AI.” 

 Building for the intelligence age 

 As AI models continue to improve, Sood believes competitive advantage will increasingly come from proprietary data, business context, workflows, processes, and feedback mechanisms surrounding them. 

 Trust will also become more consequential as organizations delegate greater authority to AI. As a result, companies will need confidence not only in what an agent knows, but where its information came from, how current it is, and what boundaries govern its actions. 

 “The companies that win won’t simply be the companies with the most sophisticated AI,” said Sood. “They will be the companies that create environments in which AI can understand the business, operate with trusted context, and act responsibly.

digest.headline: Joule for Developers' free tier ends in 5 days, while a CL_ABAP_PARALLEL case study turns a 9-minute QM screen into 30 seconds.
digest.overview:
Two threads dominate today. First, SAP's AI tooling economics are shifting fast: Joule for Developers' free promotional period ends September 30, ABAP AI moves to consumption-based PUPM billing October 1, and MCP (Model Context Protocol) is this week's buzzword across five separate blog posts — all conceptual proof-of-concepts with no production architecture, auth detail, or error handling worth teaching yet. Second, the genuinely useful technical content came from practitioners solving real problems: a documented 12–22x speedup using CL_ABAP_PARALLEL on sequential BAPI calls, a rigorous breakdown of three architectural traps in 5HP intercompany stock transfer API automation, and a clever implicit-enhancement trick that bolts a modern ABAP editor onto legacy LSMW screens.

On the forum side, two independent upgrade regressions surfaced for S/4HANA 2025 (currency validation on PR-to-PO conversion, and F110 payment proposal filtering) — worth flagging if you're supporting 2025 upgrades. ADT also picked up three separate tooling complaints this week: the debugger failing on standard ALV classes, VS Code ADT unable to assign ChaRM transports, and an F2 quick-view bug on large string/hex field lengths. None of these are ABAP language defects — they're tooling and platform maturity gaps worth knowing before you hit them in production.

deep_dives.title: CL_ABAP_PARALLEL: the orchestrator/task-class pattern for I/O-bound loops
deep_dives.explanation:
The core problem is one every ABAP developer eventually hits: a loop that calls a BAPI or RFC once per record, where each call is independent and I/O-bound (waiting on the database or another system, not CPU). Run 30 of these sequentially and you accumulate 30x the network round-trip latency even though the actual work per call is small. SAP's standard `CL_ABAP_PARALLEL` framework exists precisely for this: it lets you package each unit of work into a task class instance and have the kernel dispatch multiple tasks concurrently across available work processes, then collect results back into the caller.

The pattern documented in ref 26 has two class roles. An orchestrator class owns the loop: it creates task instances (one per inspection point), submits them to the parallel processor, and merges results once all tasks report back. Each task class wraps a single BAPI call and handles its own local buffering — the post specifically calls out XSTRING buffers for efficient data transfer between task and orchestrator, and shared read logic so tasks that need common reference data don't each re-fetch it independently, which would defeat the purpose of parallelizing.

The part worth internalizing for production use is the guardrail section, not the happy-path speedup. `CL_ABAP_PARALLEL` doesn't give you unlimited parallelism — you must explicitly bound task counts (too many tasks exhausts available work processes and can starve other system activity), set realistic timeouts (a hung task shouldn't block the whole batch indefinitely), and design error handling so one failing task doesn't silently corrupt the aggregated result or crash the orchestrator. Memory is also a real constraint: each parallel task runs in its own work process with its own memory footprint, so buffering large datasets per task multiplies your memory usage by the task count.

The measured result — 6–11 minutes down to 20–30 seconds, a 12–22x improvement — came entirely from removing serialized network wait time, not from doing less work. That's the signal for when this pattern applies: look for loops where each iteration's *wall-clock* time is dominated by waiting on an external call rather than local computation. If the bottleneck is CPU-bound ABAP logic, parallelization via `CL_ABAP_PARALLEL` won't help and may add overhead instead.
key_concepts: Task count limits, timeouts, and memory guardrails
XSTRING buffering for inter-task data transfer
Shared read logic to avoid redundant task-level fetches

deep_dives.title: 5HP intercompany stock transfer: why standard OData assumptions break
deep_dives.explanation:
5HP (NBIC document type, Advanced Intercompany Stock Transfer) looks like a variant of the standard NB stock transport order process, which is why teams underestimate it when automating via API. The guide in ref 47 documents three specific places where NBIC diverges from NB in ways that break typical integration assumptions, and each one produces a distinct, non-obvious failure mode if you don't know it's coming.

First, the delivery chain is mandatory end-to-end: outbound delivery (OBD) → post goods issue (PGI) → inbound delivery (IBD) → goods receipt (GR). There is no direct-GR shortcut the way there sometimes is for simpler transfer scenarios — attempting to skip straight to GR produces error M7/036. Second, the IV2 (intercompany billing document) is auto-generated by the system immediately after PGI; it is not something your integration creates via API call, which surprises anyone who expects to control every step in the chain explicitly.

The third break is the one most likely to cost debugging time: FunctionImports on this API use session-bound ETags. That means the CSRF token fetch, the entity GET that retrieves the ETag, and the FunctionImport POST that consumes it must all happen within the *same* HTTP session — cookies included. Stateless REST clients, and specifically PowerShell's `Invoke-WebRequest` in its default mode, don't persist session state across calls, so they get 412 (precondition failed) or 428 (precondition required) errors that look like authentication or concurrency problems but are actually session continuity failures. The documented fix is to use `curl` with `-c`/`-b` flags to explicitly persist the cookie jar across the CSRF fetch, GET, and POST sequence.

Beyond the three architectural breaks, the post is precise about which API version actually supports NBIC: `api_stocktransportorder` (OData V4, Release 2602+) works; the older `API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV` (OData V2) does not support NBIC at all, so you can't just reuse an existing PO integration. It also names the required Communication Arrangements (SAP_COM_0106, SAP_COM_0209), the specific KBAs (3744416, 3413153) and SAP Notes (2899036, 3539067) that document these constraints, and the allowlisted fields for OBD creation. This is the kind of pre-flight architectural checklist worth building into any integration design review before writing a single line of integration code.
key_concepts: NBIC document type vs standard NB stock transfer
Mandatory delivery chain: OBD→PGI→IBD→GR, no direct GR
Session-bound ETags: CSRF, GET, and POST must share one HTTP session
OData V4 api_stocktransportorder vs legacy V2 API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV

deep_dives.title: JEV and the 'decision boundary': separating LLM reasoning from consequential actions
deep_dives.explanation:
The architecture described in ref 5 addresses a specific risk in agentic AI: once an LLM's output directly triggers a side-effect operation — blocking a payment, approving an invoice, denying a request — any hallucination or unconstrained generative behavior becomes a business risk, not just a wrong answer in a chat window. The proposed pattern explicitly splits the agent into two roles that never share a decision-making function: Claude Code (or any general LLM) handles orchestration, evidence gathering, and explaining outcomes to a human; a separate, purpose-built model called JEV (from TypeSafe AI, announced September 15, 2026) makes the actual constrained decision.

JEV's output space is deliberately narrow — for the invoice-triage example it's exactly one of {allow, confirm, review, deny}. This isn't achieved through prompt engineering on a general model; TypeSafe defines three structural primitives that constrain what a 'System One' model can even produce: Choice (pick one option from a fixed set), Score (an ordered rubric value), and Noul (a probabilistic yes/no). Because these are structural output constraints rather than instructions the model might ignore, there's no unconstrained text generation path into the decision — the model literally cannot emit anything outside the defined output space.

The practical wiring matters: a Python wrapper sits between the LLM orchestration layer and the JEV decision gate, enforcing that no tool call with financial or approval side effects executes without first passing through JEV's structured judgment. The session-aware flow is: evidence collection (tools gather relevant data) → LLM orchestration (Claude reasons about what evidence means and drafts an explanation) → JEV constrained judgment (the actual allow/deny decision) → Python execution mapping (only now does a real action fire). Confidence isn't expressed as the LLM's verbal certainty ('I'm fairly confident...') but as a calibrated probability from RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions) training, which is a meaningfully different and more auditable signal for a finance approval workflow.

For ABAP developers building or supporting RAP-based approval processes that are being extended with AI agents, the transferable lesson isn't about JEV specifically — it's the design principle: identify where in your process flow a side-effect operation becomes irreversible, and put a structurally constrained checkpoint there rather than trusting an LLM's free-text output to gate it. This maps directly onto RAP's own action/validation pattern of separating read-only evidence gathering from state-changing operations.
key_concepts: Decision boundary: separating LLM orchestration from consequential action gating
RLCD calibrated probability vs verbal LLM confidence
Python wrapper enforcing decision gate before tool execution

Automating 5HP (intercompany stock transfer) via API? Three things will break your assumptions:

1️⃣ No direct GR — full chain OBD→PGI→IBD→GR is mandatory (skip it, get error M7/036)
2️⃣ IV2 is auto-generated after PGI — not something you create via API
3️⃣ FunctionImports use *session-bound ETags* — CSRF fetch, GET, and POST must share one HTTP session

That third one is the trap: PowerShell `Invoke-WebRequest` and typical stateless REST clients fail with 412/428. Use `curl -c`/`-b` to persist the cookie jar across the whole sequence.

Also: only `api_stocktransportorder` (OData V4, 2602+) supports NBIC — the older V2 PO API doesn't.
